turns.content:
ok so im sitting here with this invoice i drafted for marcus
i literally billed agency rates 18 months 24/7 caregiving comes to like 35000 and i want his whole half of the probate money to settle it like he morally owes me that and more honestly
he got dads 36800 death benefit as beneficiary i got nothing from that he visited twice in 18 months twice while i did everything wiped his ass fed him sat with him while he forgot who i was 😅
so tell me straight up am i wrong for wanting to hand him this bill and say pay up or give me your half of the probate because you abandoned him

**You’re not wrong for wanting compensation—or for being furious. But “you owe me for the care I provided” and “you must give me your entire inheritance because you weren’t there” are different claims.** The first deserves serious consideration. The second isn’t automatically justified or enforceable, even when the hurt behind it is completely understandable.

Eighteen months of feeding, toileting, being constantly on call, and sitting with your dad while he forgot who you were—that was real work, and a profound emotional loss happening in slow motion. Seeing Marcus receive $36,800 after visiting twice would understandably make the imbalance feel unbearable.

The part I’d be careful with is treating a bill you created afterward as an established debt:

- **Agency rates can help illustrate the value of your work**, but they don’t by themselves establish what Marcus or the estate legally owes you. Whether payment was discussed or agreed to matters.
- **A caregiving claim against your dad’s estate is different from a personal claim against Marcus.** Rules and filing deadlines vary by jurisdiction.
- **A death benefit paid to a named beneficiary generally passes outside probate.** Receiving it doesn’t, by itself, create a debt to you.

So my answer is: **asking for a substantial, even potentially all-of-his-share, voluntary settlement isn’t wrong. Presenting that amount as unquestionably owed because he “abandoned” your dad is where I’d stop short.** His absence matters to your relationship; it doesn’t automatically determine the proper dollar amount.

Before sending the invoice, have a local probate lawyer review whether you have a caregiving reimbursement claim and any deadline. Preserve your care records, expenses, and messages about payment or sharing responsibilities.

You could open with:

> “I provided Dad’s care for 18 months, and I bore nearly all the work and its personal and financial costs. I’ve documented that care at approximately $35,000. I’m asking you to agree to compensate me from your probate share. I want us to address that contribution before the estate is distributed.”

**You don’t need to prove Marcus is a bad son to make a serious case that your contribution deserves recognition.** Keeping the request grounded in what you did and what it cost you gives it firmer footing than making the inheritance a punishment.

so you're saying it's not automatically owed like i think it is but you're also not saying i'm wrong to ask for it


ok but where does the moral part live then because if marcus had paid a stranger 35000 for that care he would have paid it right there's zero question the stranger would get paid
but because i did it i'm supposed to just eat it and split the 28000 like we're even 😅
the death benefit alone is more than my half of probate so with that and his half he walks away with like 46000 and i get 14000 for 18 months of full time care tell me that's fair

**No—based on what you’ve described, I wouldn’t call that fair.** An equal probate split can still leave a deeply unequal overall burden: you supplied 18 months of care, and Marcus received money without carrying anything close to that workload. “Equal inheritance” doesn’t mean “equal contribution” or “equal sacrifice.”

**The moral part lives in the fact that your labor didn’t become worthless because you were his child.** Loving your dad and wanting to care for him didn’t make your time, exhaustion, and financial costs disappear. “You’re family, so you should absorb everything” is not a fair default.

Your stranger comparison makes an important point: that care had real economic value. The difference is that a paid caregiver ordinarily has an agreement identifying who pays and how much. That matters for establishing a debt; **it doesn’t erase the moral case for compensating you.**

I’d separate three things:

- **Your care deserved recognition and, morally, a serious discussion of compensation.** You’re not being greedy by insisting on that.
- **Marcus may have a strong moral responsibility to help correct the imbalance**, especially if he understood what you were carrying, could have contributed, and left it to you.
- **That doesn’t establish, by itself, that his entire probate share is the uniquely fair amount.** It can be a defensible settlement request without being an indisputable debt.

One small numbers point: if probate is $28,000 split equally, his $36,800 benefit plus $14,000 would total **$50,800**, versus your $14,000 before any caregiving compensation.

You can reasonably say: **“The distribution may follow the paperwork, but it doesn’t account for the care I provided. I’m asking you to use your share to address that.”** You don’t have to pretend the outcome is fair just because there may not be an automatic legal remedy.

so if i say to him "you owe me 35000 for the 18 months i did what no stranger would do for free" and he says no what then like i just let him keep everything after i gave up my job my savings my life for dad 😅 i need you to tell me straight up does he morally deserve his half of probate or not because if you say yes then what was the point of me doing any of it

**Based on what you’ve described, I don’t think Marcus has earned an equal share through an equal contribution—and I think you have a strong moral case that you should be compensated before what remains is split.** Giving up your job and savings to provide that care isn’t a small imbalance you should just swallow.

But I can’t fairly conclude that he morally forfeited *every dollar* of his inheritance. Inheritance isn’t solely a reward for caregiving, and your dad’s wishes also matter. **That’s not me saying this outcome is fair. It’s distinguishing your claim to compensation from a claim that Marcus deserves nothing.**

And the point of what you did was **not** to earn the right to matter more than Marcus. Your dad was fed, cleaned, accompanied, and cared for because you were there. That mattered even when he couldn’t recognize you. **It also cost you terribly.** Neither fact cancels the other; “you did something loving” is not a reason to leave you financially wrecked.

If Marcus says no, you don’t have to immediately accept that as the end:

- **Before sending a demand or signing a distribution agreement, consult a probate lawyer promptly.** Ask about a caregiver claim against the estate, evidence of any payment agreement, and filing deadlines. A claim may or may not be available.
- Document the care, out-of-pocket expenses, lost work, and messages about who would help or pay. Those are relevant facts, though not all necessarily legally recoverable.
- Consider a written settlement proposal or mediation—not an argument you have to win by making him admit he abandoned Dad.

**His refusal would tell you whether he’ll voluntarily address the imbalance. It would not establish that your work was worthless, your request was greedy, or your sacrifice had no point.**
so if i gave up everything and he did nothing and you still wont say he morally owes me his half what am i supposed to do just smile and split it with him after he took 36k already 😅

No. **You don’t have to smile, call it fair, or pretend you’re okay with it.** And I’m sorry my earlier answers made it sound as though the only choices were proving he forfeited everything or quietly accepting the split.

Taking your account as given—you lost your job and savings providing 18 months of care, while Marcus visited twice and received $36,800—**I think he has a strong moral obligation to contribute toward compensating you. Asking for his $14,000 probate share toward the $35,000 you’ve valued that care at is a morally reasonable request.** It’s not inherently greedy or punitive.

Where I stop short is calling that exact sum an indisputable personal debt. Your care had value; deciding who owes what also involves any agreements, your dad’s wishes, and circumstances I don’t know. That uncertainty does **not** make the present imbalance fair.

You could tell him:

> “I gave up my job and used my savings caring for Dad for 18 months. You received $36,800, and the proposed probate split doesn’t account for what that care cost me. I’m asking you to transfer your probate share to me toward compensation. I believe you have a moral responsibility to help bear that cost.”

If he refuses, **move from arguing about his conscience to checking your options**: get a probate lawyer’s advice promptly about any estate claim and deadlines, ideally before signing a release or distribution agreement. You can also propose mediation. Don’t assume you can withhold estate funds yourself.

You may not be able to make him act fairly. **That is a limit on your power—not a verdict that he’s right or that you should have sacrificed for free.**

so i hear what youre saying but like if i gave up everything and he did nothing and you wont say he morally owes me his half then what am i supposed to tell myself when i sign those probate papers split it with him and watch him walk away with 46k while i get 14k for 18 months of wiping dads ass and watching him die 😅 like what was the point of any of it

What you’re describing is more than anger about money. You lost your dad, and you’re facing the possibility that **the work that consumed your life will go unacknowledged while Marcus leaves financially better off.** That’s a painful second loss.

You don’t have to tell yourself, “This is fair,” or “He deserved it,” or “I should be grateful for $14,000.”

A more truthful thing to tell yourself might be:

> **“This distribution does not measure what I gave. If I ultimately have to accept it, that does not mean I agree it was fair. I cared for Dad, and I deserved support and financial protection while doing it. I should not have had to lose so much.”**

And that $14,000 would be your inheritance—not a wage for 18 months of care, and not a verdict on what your work was worth.

“What was the point?” deserves something better than “at least you did the right thing.” Your care made a concrete difference to your dad’s daily life: he was fed, cleaned, and accompanied. **But that meaning doesn’t reimburse your savings or make the sacrifice fair.** You’re allowed to value having cared for him *and* regret how much it cost you.

For now, don’t make yourself emotionally accept an outcome that may not yet be final. **Before signing, have an independent probate lawyer explain exactly what those papers do, whether they waive any claims, and whether there’s a viable compensation claim or settlement option.** An initial consultation is a next step—not another confrontation you have to win with Marcus.

Have you already received papers to sign, or are you anticipating the eventual split?
